concept.technique_name: percentile interpretation on a non-linear scale

examples.problem_statement: The 75th percentile on a test corresponded to a score of 700, while the 25th percentile corresponded to a score of 450. Quantity A: 800. Quantity B: A 95th percentile score.

solution.operation: Record the two given anchors: 25\text{th percentile} = 450,\ 75\text{th percentile} = 700
solution.result: Two fixed points on the percentile-to-score mapping, 50 percentile points apart
solution.description: Write down the only two percentile-score pairs the problem supplies, so it is clear what is actually known before any comparison is attempted.

solution.operation: Test whether the 250\text{-point gap over }50\text{ percentile points} may be extended to other percentiles
solution.result: It may not: scoring scales on a test are not necessarily linear
solution.description: Check the hidden assumption behind lining up percentile differences with score differences; because test scales need not be linear, that extrapolation is not licensed.

solution.operation: State the full information the two anchors give about the distribution: 25\% \le 450,\ 50\% \text{ between } 450 \text{ and } 700,\ 25\% > 700
solution.result: The only certain facts are these three population shares
solution.description: Convert the percentile statements into the distribution facts they guarantee, so nothing beyond them is smuggled into the comparison.

solution.operation: Compare 800 against candidate 95th percentile scores such as 750 \text{ and } 963
solution.result: Quantity B can be below 800 (750) or above 800 (963)
solution.description: Since any score above 700 is consistent with the 95th percentile, try one candidate under 800 and one over it to see that Quantity B is not pinned down.

solution.operation: Select the comparison verdict consistent with both candidates
solution.result: The relationship cannot be determined
solution.description: Because two admissible scenarios give opposite comparisons, no single relationship holds, which is the choice for an undetermined comparison.

key_reminders: A percentile tells you the share of scores above and below a value, not the spacing between scores.
Test scoring scales are not necessarily linear, so percentile gaps cannot be converted into score gaps.
In a quantitative comparison, one admissible case each way forces the undetermined answer.
common_mistakes: Treating 450 to 700 across 25th to 75th percentile as a constant 5 points per percentile and extrapolating a 95th percentile score of 800.
Assuming the scores are normally distributed and reading the 95th percentile off a bell curve, when no distribution is given.

examples.problem_statement: A four digit number wxyz is such that x + y = 2w, y + 6z = 2(w + x) and w + 5z = 2y. Find the sum of such four digit numbers which satisfy the given conditions.

solution.operation: Number the constraints: x + y = 2w \ (1),\quad y + 6z = 2(w + x)\ (2),\quad w + 5z = 2y\ (3)
solution.result: Three linear equations in the four digits w, x, y, z
solution.description: Label each printed condition so the eliminations that follow can refer to them by number.

solution.result: x = 2z
solution.description: Subtract the first equation from the second; the y terms cancel and the right side leaves 2x, giving x directly in terms of z.

solution.operation: Substitute x = 2z into (1):\quad 2z + y = 2w
solution.description: Put the relation just found back into equation (1) to get a new equation (4) in w, y and z only.

solution.operation: Solve (3) and (4) together:\quad w + 5z = 2y,\ 2w - y = 2z
solution.result: w = 3z,\ y = 4z
solution.description: Combine the two remaining equations to express w and y as multiples of z, so every digit is now a multiple of z.

solution.operation: Read off z : y : x : w = 1 : 4 : 2 : 3 and take the admissible digit multiples
solution.result: z = 1 gives 3241 and z = 2 gives 6482
solution.description: Scale the ratio by z; only z = 1 and z = 2 keep every digit in range, producing the two four-digit numbers that satisfy all three conditions.
Add the two qualifying numbers, since the question asks for the sum of all such four-digit numbers.

key_reminders: Subtracting one condition from another to cancel a shared digit term is the fastest route into these digit puzzles.
Once all digits are multiples of z, only the values of z that keep every digit a single digit are admissible.
The question asks for the sum of all qualifying numbers, not for one number.
common_mistakes: Stopping at one solution (3241 or 6482) and reporting it instead of their sum.
Accepting z = 3, which forces y = 12 and is not a digit.

examples.problem_statement: Mahesh got Rs 1200 as dividend from a finance co. What is the rate of interest given by the company? Which of the given statements is/are sufficient/necessary? A. Mahesh has 960 shares of Rs 10 denomination. B. The dividend paid last year was 9.5%.

solution.operation: From statement A: 960 \times 10
solution.result: Invested capital = Rs 9600
solution.description: Multiply the number of shares by the face value given in statement A to obtain the capital on which the dividend was paid.

solution.operation: Form the rate from the dividend and that capital: \dfrac{1200}{9600}
solution.result: The rate is determined, so A alone is sufficient
solution.description: Divide the known dividend by the capital just computed; because both quantities are now known, statement A settles the rate on its own.

solution.operation: Test statement B: last year's dividend rate of 9.5\% against this year's rate
solution.result: Last year's dividend need not equal this year's, so B is not sufficient
solution.description: Check whether the prior year's rate constrains the current year; it does not, so statement B contributes nothing to the required rate.

solution.operation: Match the finding (A sufficient, B not) to the printed options
solution.result: Only A is sufficient
solution.description: Pick the option that says A alone suffices, since one statement worked and the other did not.

key_reminders: Dividend rate is computed on the face value of the holding: capital = number of shares x denomination.
A rate from a previous year is not evidence about the current year's rate.
common_mistakes: Reading 'rate of interest' as needing a market price and declaring A insufficient, when the Rs 10 denomination already fixes the capital.
Assuming the 9.5% of statement B carries over to this year and calling B sufficient.

examples.problem_statement: Grace's average bowling score over the past 6 games is 150. If she wants to raise her average score by 10%, and she has two more games remaining in the season, what must her average score on the last two games be?

solution.description: Take 10 percent of the current average, because the target is an average raised by that percentage.

solution.result: Target average = 165 over all 8 games
solution.description: Add the increase to the current average to get the average Grace must hold across the whole season.

solution.operation: Original scenario row: 150 \times 6
solution.result: Sum of the first 6 games = 900
solution.description: Fill the first row of the average table, converting the known average and game count into the points already scored.

solution.operation: Final two games row: A \times 2 = 2A;\ targeted outcome row: 165 \times 8 = 900 + 2A
solution.description: Write the last two games with unknown average A, then set the eight-game total from the target average equal to the old sum plus those two games.

solution.operation: 2A = 1320 - 900 = 420 \Rightarrow A = \dfrac{420}{2}
solution.description: Solve the last row of the table for A by isolating the two-game sum and halving it, giving the required average for the final two games.

key_reminders: Average x number of terms = sum; build a row per scenario and keep the sums consistent.
A percentage increase in an average is taken on the original average, here 10% of 150.
The target average applies to all 8 games, not just the remaining 2.
common_mistakes: Raising the target only over the 2 remaining games, i.e. answering 165 instead of 210.
Using 6 games instead of 8 in the target row and getting a sum of 990.

concept.technique_name: conditional rule application in a basic grouping game

examples.problem_statement: On a field trip to the Museum of Natural History, each of six children - Juana, Kyle, Lucita, Salim, Thanh, and Veronica - is accompanied by one of three adults - Ms. Margoles, Mr. O'Connell, and Ms. Podorski. Each adult accompanies exactly two of the children, consistent with the following conditions: If Ms. Margoles accompanies Juana, then Ms. Podorski accompanies Lucita. If Kyle is not accompanied by Ms. Margoles, then Veronica is accompanied by Mr. O'Connell. Either Ms. Margoles or Mr. O'Connell accompanies Thanh. Juana is not accompanied by the same adult as Kyle; nor is Lucita accompanied by the same adult as Salim; nor is Thanh accompanied by the same adult as Veronica. Mr. O'Connell CANNOT accompany which one of the following pairs of children?

solution.operation: Classify the answer choices: four pairs CAN be assigned to O, exactly one CANNOT
solution.result: The task is to find the single pair that breaks a rule when placed in O's column
solution.description: Read the question as an exception question so the search is for the one violating pair rather than for a full valid arrangement.

solution.operation: Identify the rule that governs O's column: \text{not } V_O \rightarrow K_M
solution.result: Whenever V is not with O, K must be with M
solution.description: Since the question is about O's column, isolate the conditional that fires on O, and note it triggers precisely for choices that do not contain V.

solution.operation: Test (A): place J and L with O
solution.result: K can go to M, and T and V can be kept apart - no violation
solution.description: Try the first V-free choice and check the conditional and the separation rules; an arrangement exists, so (A) is not the answer.

solution.operation: Test (C): place K and T with O, which also omits V
solution.result: V not with O forces K into M, yet (C) puts K with O - contradiction
solution.description: Apply the same conditional to the other V-free choice; the trigger demands K in M while the choice itself places K with O, so the pair is impossible.

solution.operation: Select the pair shown to be impossible in O's column
solution.result: Kyle and Thanh cannot both be with Mr. O'Connell
solution.description: Report the choice whose placement was contradicted, since it is the only pair that cannot be assigned to O.

key_reminders: In a CANNOT question, one choice must break a rule while the other four are constructible.
Target the conditional whose trigger involves the group the question asks about, here the rule firing when V is not with O.
The contrapositive matters: V not in O's column forces K into Margoles' column.
common_mistakes: Skipping the V-free choices and testing (B) or (E), where the conditional never fires and no contradiction appears.
Reading the rule as 'V must be with O' rather than as the conditional that forces K into M.
